A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RLRE study. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–H are readable and support reliable matching across additions, renumbering, and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original model-training experiments, MT-Bench evaluations, transfer and ablation studies, and human attack-detection results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds further judge evaluations, Arena-Hard results, and a human response-quality study.

M1.justification: RLRE retains the same upstream preamble generator, frozen candidate and judge models, adapted CoPG loss, and inference procedure. The instructions in Appendix E are unchanged. Expanded explanations of beta and the proposed future use of multiple judges do not establish a procedural change.

E1.justification: v2 adds actual evaluation on Arena-Hard, previously only discussed, extending coverage to a different task distribution beyond MT-Bench. UltraFeedback training and MT-Bench evaluation remain.

E2.justification: The five attack baselines in Table 2 remain unchanged. However, the per-domain comparison expands from refinement, universal attack, and preambles in v1 Table 9 to also include no attack, verbosity, bandwagon, and authority in v2 Table 11.

E3.justification: The human detection study expands from 175 responses and seven annotators to 400 responses and sixteen annotators. v2 adds blinded categorical and 1–10 human quality ratings, extends accuracy assessment to all three candidates with explicitly stated normalized exact match, and introduces GPT-4o-mini/Claude judge evaluations and Arena-Hard's 0–100 scoring protocol. Existing training hyperparameters and selected checkpoints remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a human study testing whether higher judge scores reflect better response quality and broadens the math/reasoning accuracy check across candidates. Transfer robustness and human detectability evidence also expand. The input-conditioning ablations, random-string control, and response-layout examples are retained; the random-string control moves to Appendix G.4.

E5.justification: v2 introduces paired-bootstrap confidence intervals for attack effects and Spearman/Kendall agreement statistics with p-values for the new human quality study. Five-run means, standard deviations, and detection-study MAD were already reported in v1. The new intervals' confidence level is inconsistent: Appendix D.1 says 90%, while Table 10 says 95%.

E6.justification: Table 2's results remain unchanged, but v2 adds judge-transfer scores, per-domain baseline entries, human quality ratings, and Arena-Hard results: without/with preambles, 58.3/61.8 under Command R+ and 27.6/28.8 under GPT-4. Under expanded study settings, preamble detection changes from 20% to 14%, and the accuracy summary changes from 25%/25% for Command R7B to 45.9%/44.2% across all candidates. Llama's math preamble standard deviation also changes from 0.08 to 0.12.

T1.justification: The expected-reward objective and CoPG loss retain their mathematical substance. Writing the expectation over q alone in v2 is consistent with the instruction already being fixed in v1. No substantive new assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The abstract and six listed contributions retain their central claims. The conclusion extends transferability to multiple benchmarks and explicitly emphasizes indirect optimization of models that cannot be fine-tuned directly. Cross-judge effectiveness wording also becomes less absolute than v1's claim of equal effectiveness.

C2.justification: v2 extends the score-inflation interpretation through human quality assessments and adds a model-family/low-beta explanation for differing preamble fluency in Appendix G.4. Appendix B.4 discusses cost and API constraints on training with multiple judges, while Appendix D.3 qualifies the GPT-4 Arena-Hard improvement relative to reported variation.

D1.justification: Appendix B.3 newly documents a maximum of 128,000 judge queries and an approximately $500 API cost estimate. Appendix F.2 provides quality-annotation instructions. Broader Impacts explicitly states that trained checkpoints are not released; v1 provides no corresponding availability statement, so withdrawal of previously available models is not established.

R1.justification: v2 adds model-documentation references and discussion of attention- and distribution-based detection methods, while removing the Length-controlled AlpacaEval and WildBench references. The central positioning against post hoc attacks and the reliance on CoPG remain unchanged. Publication and title updates to retained references do not constitute new works.

P1.justification: v2 edits and condenses prose throughout the existing narrative, fixes the unresolved Table ?? reference, and adds acknowledgments. New material is organized into additional appendix subsections, but the main section sequence and overall organization remain stable.

P2.justification: The results displays expand substantially: Table 3(b) gains two judge columns, and the per-domain table grows from three to seven conditions. New Tables 6, 10, and 12 present human quality, confidence intervals, and Arena-Hard results. Figure 3 is updated and relocated with Table 4; the pipeline diagram and radar plots retain their designs.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence separating score inflation from genuine quality improvement relied mainly on a Command R7B math/reasoning check. v2 substantially strengthens this central distinction through blinded human quality ratings across domains, broader accuracy checks, and additional judge and benchmark transfer evidence. Human ratings remain nearly equal at 6.22 versus 6.24 despite higher judge scores. The inconsistent confidence-level labeling and weak GPT-4 Arena-Hard evidence limit some conclusions, but do not outweigh the stronger validation.
